title: Tales in stone
hookLine: Jataka carvings at Bharhut and Borobudur, paintings on the cave walls at Ajanta

lines: THE TALE'S NAME, CUT IN STONE.
cards: A stone post, its faces carved with round panels. On one round panel, a deer kneels in front of a king. On another, monkeys cross a river on a bridge made of their own bodies.
Next to some of the panels, a few letters are cut into the stone: the name of the tale. Somebody, long ago, wanted to make sure you knew which story you were looking at.
This is the railing of a stupa at Bharhut, in India.

teach.h: THE NAME CARVED BESIDE THE PICTURE.
teach.b: The carvers at Bharhut didn't only show the tales; on some panels they carved the tale's name beside the picture. So a scene of animals and kings isn't a guess.
The stone tells you which birth story it is, and scholars can match it with the tales we still read.
On the island of Java stands Borobudur, a huge Buddhist monument built in terraces, its galleries lined with carved panels, among them birth stories.
Pilgrims walk around it, keeping the monument on their right, and the stories unfold beside them, scene after scene, climbing level by level.
You read it with your feet.

In western India, at Ajanta, halls were cut straight into a cliff, and their walls were painted with scenes from the Buddha's lives: a white elephant among lotus pools, a prince and his court, crowds and palaces, all on rock.
Why put tales in stone at all?

teach.h: A TALE FOR ANYONE WHO CAN SEE.
teach.b: A carving teaches anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. A monk or a parent could stand at a panel and tell the story while pointing to it.
And stone lasts. The tales we've been hearing were told aloud and copied, and also cut into rock and painted on walls in places far apart.

The six-tusked elephant you met a few days ago stands on a railing at Bharhut and on a painted wall at Ajanta. When you hear a Jataka, you are hearing something people once walked past, touched and pointed at.

how: Buddhist pilgrims walk around stupas and monuments with the shrine on their right, and at places like Borobudur the carved birth stories line the path they walk.

o: a story of one of the Buddha's past lives
a carved railing around a stupa
a book of rules for monks and nuns

games.q: tales in stone: tap the pairs.
p: the tale's name carved beside the picture
panels you walk past, level by level
scenes painted on walls cut into a cliff

s: the Jataka survived only as written books
the tales were also carved on stupa railings and monuments and painted on cave walls.
at Bharhut, some panels carry the name of the tale
a few carved letters beside the scene say which birth story it is.
Borobudur is on the island of Java. Bharhut and Ajanta are in India.

games.q: you're a carver with one round panel to fill, and the tale you've been given is long. what do you carve?
o: the whole tale, squeezed in tiny.
one moment, with the tale's name cut beside it.
a plain pattern, and let a teacher tell the story.
games.why: at Bharhut, carvers chose a key scene, and on some panels they added the tale's name so no one would guess wrong.

practice: If you have a screen nearby, find a photograph of one panel from Bharhut, Borobudur or Ajanta and simply look at it: who is in it, and what moment did the carver choose?
If you'd rather not look anything up, pick one tale from these weeks and picture it as a single carved scene, then close your eyes and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Jataka. The birth stories carved and painted at Bharhut, Borobudur and Ajanta, for anyone who could see. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a birth story, a tale of one of the Buddha's earlier lives.

carryVoice: Your line: the tales in stone. Stone kept the stories for people who never read them. That's day eight hundred forty-nine.
